title: Censure: Punishment Without Removal
hook: Legislatures mostly cannot fire their own members easily — voters hired them. So they built a middle sanction: a formal, recorded statement that the chamber disapproves.
key_points: Legislatures discipline members internally because members are elected, not appointed, so removal would override voters.
The usual ladder runs from reprimand, to censure, to expulsion — with expulsion typically needing a supermajority and being rare.
Censure is a formal vote of disapproval placed on the record; it does not remove a member or strip their vote.
Its force is reputational and procedural — it can accompany loss of committee posts and becomes a permanent part of a member's record.

In September 2026 the House formally censured Rep. Chuck Edwards of North Carolina after a House Ethics Committee investigation into sexual harassment allegations involving two young staff members, per NPR.
NPR reports the censure vote drew bipartisan support — a signal that matters, since internal discipline is credible only when it crosses party lines.
content_html: A legislature has an awkward problem with misbehaving members: it did not hire them. Voters did. Removing someone the electorate chose is a serious step, so most chambers reserve expulsion for extreme cases and rely on a graded set of lesser sanctions instead.
extra_html: Censure sits in the middle of that ladder — above a reprimand, below expulsion. It is a formal vote putting the chamber's disapproval on the permanent record, and it can be paired with practical consequences such as losing a committee chairmanship, but it leaves the member in office with their vote intact. Its power is reputational: a recorded judgment by colleagues that follows a member into the next campaign. NPR's Claudia Grisales reports that in September 2026 the House censured Rep. Chuck Edwards of North Carolina following a House Ethics Committee investigation into allegations of sexual harassment against two young female staff members, and that the vote drew bipartisan support. That last detail carries weight beyond the case. Self-policing is always vulnerable to the objection that it is just the majority punishing the minority; a cross-party vote is the main evidence a chamber can offer that it is applying a standard rather than a strategy. (This card describes the U.S. House specifically; other legislatures use similar ladders under different names.)

related.title: The Legislature
related.hook: The branch that makes the law is also where a society argues out loud — the legislature turns competing interests into binding rules through debate and votes.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: There's No 25th Amendment for Congress
related.hook: When a president is incapacitated, the Constitution has a formal fix: the 25th Amendment. When a senator is hospitalized for weeks with no details given, there isn't one.

related.title: Firing an Official Can Require a Hearing First
related.hook: The fight over removing a Federal Reserve governor turned on something narrower than presidential power: whether she gets told the charge and a chance to answer before she is out.

flashcards.prompt: What does a censure do to a legislator, and what does it not do?
flashcards.back_html: It records the chamber's formal disapproval and can come with loss of committee posts. It does not remove the member or take away their vote — only expulsion or the voters can do that.

flashcards.prompt: Why do legislatures discipline members internally rather than simply removing them?

choices.text: Members are elected, so removal overrides the voters who chose them
Courts are constitutionally barred from hearing any case about a legislator
Legislators cannot be investigated at all while in office

flashcards.explanation_html: That tension is why expulsion is rare and usually needs a supermajority, leaving censure as the workable middle sanction.

flashcards.prompt: Why does bipartisan support for a censure vote matter?

choices.text: Internal discipline is credible only when it is not purely a party attack
Censure legally requires votes from both parties
A bipartisan censure automatically triggers expulsion

flashcards.explanation_html: A chamber policing its own is judged on whether it applies the same standard regardless of party — which is why NPR notes the cross-party vote.
